strengths: The paper targets an important and timely bottleneck: latency of next-token autoregressive image generation, especially at high resolutions where token counts become large.

The core idea of combining low-resolution drafting, learned up/down-sampling, relaxed visual-token verification, and local rejection expansion is plausible and reasonably original within speculative decoding for image synthesis.
The evaluation includes relevant baselines adapted to the same Tar-1.5B setting, including EAGLE-2, LANTERN, and ZipAR, and reports speed, GenEval, DPG-Bench, FID, and HPSv2 rather than speed alone.

The reported gains over speculative decoding baselines are consistent: MuLo-SD improves speedup over LANTERN from 1.08x to 1.22x at 512p and from 1.42x to 1.68x at 1024p while keeping semantic metrics in a similar range.

The ablations are useful: they examine up/down-sampler losses, probability pooling, local verification, and local expansion radius, supporting that the final design is not an arbitrary combination of components.
The supplementary material provides substantial implementation detail, including sampler architectures, training steps, hyperparameters, latency breakdowns, and additional qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The main speedups are modest in absolute terms and the strongest non-speculative baseline, ZipAR, substantially outperforms MuLo-SD: 1.88x vs. 1.22x at 512p and 3.65x vs. 1.68x at 1024p with comparable or better metrics. This weakens the broader practical claim, even if the method is competitive within speculative decoding.

The proposed verification rule is no longer exact speculative decoding. Acceptance by thresholded pooled probability and retaining distant tokens after local resampling can change the target distribution, but the paper provides no formal bound for the full MuLo-SD procedure analogous to standard speculative decoding or LANTERN's TVD discussion.

Quality tradeoffs are mixed. At the reported operating points, MuLo-SD improves speed over LANTERN but has worse FID at both 512p and 1024p and worse HPSv2 at 1024p; the claim of maintaining comparable perceptual quality is only partially supported.

The experimental scope is narrow: all main experiments use Tar-1.5B and its AR-DTok checkpoints. It remains unclear whether the method transfers to other visual AR models, tokenizers, codebooks, model scales, or prompt distributions.

The comparison to LANTERN and EAGLE-2 depends on newly trained/adapted drafters whose quality is much lower than in the original LANTERN setting. The supplementary discusses this, but it still leaves uncertainty about whether the baseline adaptation is equally optimized.

The method requires training additional up- and down-samplers for each scale, which reduces the simplicity of an inference-time acceleration method. The paper does not fully analyze this added engineering/training cost relative to the achieved latency gains.

Some claims are overstated, such as 'state-of-the-art in speculative decoding for image synthesis' and 'bridging the gap between efficiency and fidelity,' given the limited model coverage and the fact that a locality-based decoding baseline dominates the speed-quality Pareto front.

Reproducibility is moderate rather than strong: many details are given, but the manuscript references a project page without a visible URL in the extracted text, and exact code/checkpoints for trained samplers and adapted baselines would be important for reproducing the reported tradeoffs.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: reducing latency for autoregressive image generation, especially at high token counts where sequential decoding is a real bottleneck.

The main idea of using a lower-resolution AR model plus learned upsampling as a drafter is intuitive and reasonably motivated by image hierarchy; the local rejection/resampling heuristic is also a plausible way to exploit spatial structure.
The experimental section includes several relevant baselines, including EAGLE-2, LANTERN, and ZipAR, and reports multiple metrics covering speed, semantic alignment, and perceptual quality.

The ablations are useful: the paper studies up/down-sampler training losses, probability pooling, local rejection/expansion, and neighborhood radius, which helps identify which parts of the method matter.
The supplementary gives some implementation details, latency breakdowns, and hyperparameters, making the method more understandable than the main text alone.
weaknesses: The central technical formulation is not fully convincing. The proposed acceptance rule uses a probability-mass threshold rather than the standard speculative decoding acceptance ratio, and accepted upsampled tokens are not sampled from the target distribution. This makes the method a heuristic approximation, not a principled speculative sampler. The paper still leans on speculative decoding language and TVD discussion from LANTERN, but does not provide an equivalent correctness or bias bound for MuLo-SD.

Local verification is especially concerning: tokens after a rejection can be kept if outside the local expansion region, even though their target-model verification logits were computed under a draft prefix that may no longer match the resampled target prefix. This may be empirically acceptable, but the paper does not analyze or quantify the resulting distributional error.

The empirical gains are modest and narrowly framed. MuLo-SD improves over the authors' port of LANTERN, but only reaches 1.22x at 512p and 1.68x at 1024p, while ZipAR achieves 1.88x and 3.65x with similar or better metric preservation. Calling the method state-of-the-art is therefore overstated unless restricted very narrowly to the authors' definition of speculative decoding.

The comparison to LANTERN is not fully satisfying. The authors report that their Tar-adapted LANTERN drafter has much lower Top-1 accuracy than in the LANTERN paper and acknowledge that the training dataset differs. This makes the strength of the claimed improvement over LANTERN uncertain.

Evaluation breadth is limited. Experiments are essentially on one base model family, one dataset split for FID/HPSv2, batch size 1 on A100, and selected operating points chosen to match LANTERN's GenEval. There is no human evaluation, no robustness study across prompts beyond benchmark averages, and no demonstration on other AR image generators or unified MLLMs.

Some latency accounting weakens the practical claim: the 17s MLLM conditioning stage is excluded, although it is part of end-to-end text-to-image generation in the described system. Including it would substantially reduce the apparent user-facing speedup, especially at 512p.

The quality tradeoff is not consistently favorable. At the reported 1024p operating point, MuLo-SD loses 0.8 GenEval, 0.3 DPG-Bench, worsens FID by 0.4, and loses 1.1 HPSv2 relative to Tar, while ZipAR preserves metrics better and is much faster.

Several presentation and reproducibility issues remain: the project page is blank in the abstract, some figure/table text is hard to parse, there are typos and notation inconsistencies, and important choices such as the 1024p expansion radius are transferred from 512p due to limited compute rather than validated.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck: accelerating next-token autoregressive image generation without changing the target model architecture. The proposed combination of low-resolution drafting, learned up/down-sampling, and locality-aware verification is well motivated for image tokens.

The method is empirically stronger than adapted speculative decoding baselines on the evaluated Tar-1.5B setting: MuLo-SD improves speedup over LANTERN at comparable GenEval scores, reaching 1.22x at 512p and 1.68x at 1024p while keeping semantic metrics close to the base model.

The evaluation is fairly broad for a systems-style decoding paper: it reports semantic alignment, perceptual quality, latency, qualitative examples, and ablations for up/down-sampler losses, probability pooling, local rejection, and neighborhood expansion.

The supplement provides useful implementation detail, including sampler training, hyperparameters, latency breakdowns, and additional comparisons, which improves reproducibility relative to many inference-method submissions.

The contribution is original enough: prior image speculative decoding addresses token ambiguity, while this work explicitly exploits image scale hierarchy and spatial locality inside the draft/verify loop.
weaknesses: The sampling procedure is approximate and the paper does not provide a strong theoretical characterization of the distributional error introduced by the threshold-based acceptance rule and local expansion. This is a material limitation because the method is framed as speculative decoding, where exactness or controlled bias is often central.

The empirical case is mostly tied to one base model family, Tar-1.5B, with one low-resolution drafter setting. It is therefore unclear how well the method transfers to other AR image generators, codebooks, stronger/weaker targets, or different tokenizer resolutions.

The strongest overall acceleration baseline, ZipAR, substantially outperforms MuLo-SD in speed-quality tradeoff, especially at 1024p. The paper correctly notes that ZipAR is orthogonal rather than speculative decoding, but this still tempers the practical impact claim.

The LANTERN and EAGLE-2 baselines are ported and retrained in a setting where they perform poorly, including negative speedups for EAGLE-2. The authors discuss this, but the comparison remains somewhat hard to interpret because the adapted drafter quality is much worse than reported in the original LANTERN setting.

Latency reporting excludes the MLLM conditioning stage, even though the text occasionally uses broad language such as end-to-end generation. The speedups are still meaningful for AR-DTok decoding, but the real user-visible gain is smaller when prompt-conditioning latency is included.

Quality tradeoffs are not uniformly favorable: MuLo-SD worsens FID relative to the base model at both resolutions and reduces HPSv2 by about 0.7-1.1. The chosen operating point matches semantic alignment reasonably well, but the perceptual degradation should be presented less optimistically.

Some important design choices are underexplored, including the local expansion radius at 1024p, the sensitivity to k and delta, and the cost/benefit of training the up/down-samplers. The supplement notes resource constraints for the 1024p radius ablation, which leaves a small but real gap.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely bottleneck: inference latency for next-token autoregressive image generation, especially at high resolutions where token counts grow quickly.

The proposed combination of low-resolution drafting, upsampling, local rejection/expansion, and parallel resampling is a plausible and useful adaptation of speculative decoding to spatial image structure. The locality idea is well motivated by recent AR image decoding work.

The empirical results on Tar-1.5B and Tar-7B are promising: MULO-SD reports about 1.9-2.0x speedup at 512p and 3.9-5.3x at 1024p while largely preserving GenEval/DPG-Bench scores, with useful ablations for upsampling, probability pooling, local expansion, and parallel decoding.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes an algorithm, latency breakdowns, qualitative comparisons, and supplementary details on training the up/downsamplers and LANTERN-style drafters.
weaknesses: The method is no longer exact speculative decoding. The acceptance rule is a threshold on pooled target probability, and local/island resampling assumes spatial conditional independence that is not guaranteed by the AR factorization. This is acceptable as an approximate decoder, but the paper sometimes inherits speculative-decoding language without clearly characterizing the induced distributional bias or providing a bound for the full MULO-SD procedure.

The comparison to ZipAR is overstated. MULO-SD incorporates ZipAR-like parallel decoding in key stages, while ZipAR alone is already very strong: at 1024p it has better or comparable perceptual metrics than MULO-SD in Table 1, and at 512p LlamaGen it is both faster and at least as good. The claim of outperforming parallel decoding baselines is therefore only partially supported.

The strongest speedups are reported mainly on Tar at 1024p; generality is weaker. On LlamaGen-XL 512p, MULO-SD is slower than LANTERN and ZipAR and has lower semantic scores, and there is no LlamaGen 1024p experiment.

Latency reporting excludes the MLLM conditioning cost for Tar, which the supplement says is about 17 seconds. Since 512p AR-DTok decoding is about 18 seconds, the claimed speedups can materially overstate full end-to-end generation acceleration for some settings.

The LANTERN/EAGLE-2 baselines appear difficult to port and underperform substantially; the paper gives some justification, but this leaves uncertainty about whether the speculative decoding baselines are optimally tuned or fairly represented in the new Tar setting.

Quality preservation is not fully convincing. HPSv2 often drops, FID behavior is mixed and sometimes improves despite visible qualitative differences, and there is no human preference study or stronger perceptual analysis to validate that the accelerated samples are truly comparable.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: the project page placeholder is blank, code availability is unclear, and reproducing the method requires multiple resolution-specific checkpoints, an external pixel super-resolution model or trained latent upsamplers, and many hyperparameters such as tau, k, delta, and expansion radius.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck: slow sequential decoding in autoregressive image generation, especially at high resolutions where token counts become large.

The core intuition of using a lower-resolution visual AR model as a multi-scale drafter is reasonable and well matched to image structure. The local rejection/expansion idea is also a plausible way to exploit spatial locality rather than treating image tokens as a flat language sequence.
The experimental section includes several relevant baselines, including ZipAR, EAGLE-2, and LANTERN, and evaluates on multiple models/resolutions: LlamaGen-XL, Tar-1.5B, Tar-7B, 512p, and 1024p.

The paper provides useful ablations for upsampler design, probability pooling, local rejection/expansion, and parallel decoding, which help identify which parts of the pipeline contribute to the observed speedups.
The reported 1024p speedups for Tar models are practically interesting, especially the 5.33x result for Tar-7B, if the approximation-quality tradeoff is acceptable for the intended use case.
weaknesses: The method is no longer speculative decoding in the usual distribution-preserving sense. The acceptance rule in Eq. 5 uses a fixed probability-mass threshold rather than the target/draft ratio, and the local rejection/parallel island resampling heuristic has no proof or convincing bound showing that it samples from, or stays close to, the target model distribution. This is a material technical gap because the paper repeatedly frames the contribution as speculative decoding while relying on approximate, threshold-tuned acceptance.

The local verification procedure appears potentially inconsistent with autoregressive conditioning. Target logits are computed under prefixes containing draft tokens, but later only local neighborhoods around rejected tokens are resampled while distant accepted tokens after a rejection can remain fixed despite being accepted under a possibly invalid context. The paper motivates this by locality but does not quantify the error or provide a rigorous condition under which this is safe.

The main claim of outperforming ZipAR is not well supported. In Table 1, ZipAR is often competitive or better in quality-speed tradeoff: at 1024p Tar-1.5B it gives 3.65x with essentially unchanged FID/HPS, while MULO-SD gives 3.90x with worse HPS and FID; at 512p Tar-1.5B and Tar-7B the speedup advantage over ZipAR is small. The larger Tar-7B 1024p speedup comes with a large FID degradation of 3.1 and HPS drop of 0.8.

The comparison protocol favors the proposed method in places. MULO-SD incorporates ZipAR-style parallel decoding internally, but is compared against standalone ZipAR, making it hard to isolate whether the gain comes from the proposed multi-scale/local verification or from the reused parallel decoder. The paper also selects operating points by matching LANTERN GenEval rather than presenting a neutral Pareto comparison in the main table.

The reported speedups exclude the 17s MLLM conditioning latency for Tar, even though this is substantial relative to 512p decoding and still meaningful for 1024p. This makes the practical end-to-end acceleration less clear than the headline speedup numbers suggest.

The quality degradation is under-discussed. At 1024p Tar-7B, MULO-SD has nearly unchanged semantic metrics but much worse FID, similar to LANTERN; this suggests visible distributional or perceptual drift. Qualitative examples are limited and do not convincingly rule out artifacts from the approximate resampling scheme.

The baseline implementation of LANTERN appears weak and possibly not fully comparable. The authors report much lower drafter accuracy than LANTERN on LlamaGen and attribute it to Tar being stronger, but the training data and setup differ and no stronger tuning or alternative drafter capacity is shown. This weakens conclusions about outperforming speculative decoding baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The method depends on multiple checkpoints, an upsampler/downsampler, a pixel-space super-resolution model, ZipAR integration, threshold sweeps, and codebook-neighbor pooling, but many implementation details needed to reproduce exact results are either deferred or only partially specified. The project page field is blank in the PDF.

The paper has several presentation and polish issues, including typos, inconsistent capitalization of MULO-SD/MuLo-SD, awkward notation, and some claims that overstate the evidence. These are secondary to the technical concerns but reinforce the impression that the submission is not yet mature.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck: slow next-token autoregressive image generation at high resolution, especially for unified multimodal models where next-scale training objectives may not apply directly.

The core idea is well motivated and reasonably original: combining low-resolution drafting, upsampling, spatially local verification, and island-wise/ZipAR-style parallel resampling exploits image structure more directly than token-level speculative decoding.

The empirical results are promising. On Tar-1.5B/7B, MULO-SD generally improves over LANTERN and EAGLE-2 in speed-quality tradeoff, with especially strong 1024p acceleration reported up to 5.33x while preserving GenEval/DPG-Bench reasonably well.

The paper includes useful ablations for upsampler design, probability pooling, local rejection/expansion, parallel decoding, and expansion radius, which support the claim that the individual components matter.
The manuscript is mostly clear, with intuitive diagrams and a helpful supplement containing algorithmic details, latency breakdowns, and additional qualitative examples.
The limitations section is candid about practical costs from requiring separate low-resolution and high-resolution checkpoints and KV caches.
weaknesses: The sampling procedure is no longer exact speculative decoding. The acceptance rule based on a fixed probability-mass threshold and the decision to keep spatially distant accepted tokens after local resampling introduce distributional bias, but the paper provides no formal characterization or bound for the full MULO-SD sampler. This weakens claims about maintaining target-model quality.

The headline speedups overstate end-to-end user-visible acceleration for Tar because the reported latency excludes the MLLM conditioning stage, which the supplement says takes about 17 seconds. Including this cost would substantially reduce the effective speedup, especially for 512p and even for 1024p.

The comparison to LANTERN is somewhat fragile. The authors had to retrain/port LANTERN to Tar, the original LANTERN training dataset is not known, and the resulting drafter accuracy is much lower than reported for LlamaGen. This makes the magnitude of the claimed advantage over LANTERN less conclusive.

The strongest baseline, ZipAR, is very competitive and in some cases comparable or better in quality-speed tradeoff. The supplement even states that ZipAR dominates all other methods on some Pareto plots, so the paper should be more careful in claiming overall state-of-the-art acceleration.

Evaluation breadth is moderate rather than comprehensive. Results focus mainly on Tar and one LlamaGen setting, with limited analysis across prompt types, seeds, hardware, memory footprint, batch sizes, and failure cases. The method may be most compelling in the 256p-to-1024p setting, but less so at 512p or with less aligned model pairs.

Reproducibility has gaps: the project page placeholder is empty in the manuscript, exact operating points for threshold sweeps are not always tabulated, and the method depends on implementation details such as upsampler choice, connected-component resampling, ZipAR integration, and trained auxiliary modules.

Some presentation issues remain, including minor typos and inconsistent capitalization of MULO-SD/MuLo-SD, and a few claims such as “without compromising quality” are stronger than the reported metric drops and qualitative discussion support.
